title: Distributed Computing Basics
tagline: When one computer isn't enough, split the work across many that talk to each other.
what_it_is: Distributed computing splits a large task across multiple machines (a cluster) that work in parallel and coordinate with each other, rather than relying on a single powerful computer to do everything alone.
key_points: A cluster is a group of connected machines (nodes) working together as one system.
Work is split into smaller chunks distributed across nodes, processed in parallel, and results are combined.
Coordination and communication between nodes (networking, failure handling) adds real complexity that single-machine computing doesn't have.
Fault tolerance is essential — with many machines, some will fail, and the system must keep working anyway.
This is the foundational idea underneath Hadoop, Spark, and most big data infrastructure.
why_it_exists: Buying one increasingly powerful machine (scaling vertically) eventually hits physical and cost limits. Distributed computing exists to scale horizontally instead — adding more ordinary machines rather than one impossibly powerful one — to handle data and computation at a scale no single machine could manage.
intuition: One person alone could never count every grain of sand on a beach in a day. But split the beach into sections and hand each section to a different person with a clear counting method and a way to report back their subtotal, and the job becomes achievable — as long as everyone can coordinate and someone can handle it if one counter gets tired and drops out.
when_to_use: Use distributed computing when a dataset or computation genuinely doesn't fit or finish in reasonable time on one machine.
Use it when you need fault tolerance — the system should survive individual machine failures without losing work.
when_not_to_use: Do not distribute a workload that easily fits and runs fast on a single machine — the coordination overhead can make it slower, not faster.
Do not assume distributing automatically means faster — network communication between nodes can become the new bottleneck.
common_mistakes: Underestimating the complexity of coordinating and debugging failures across many machines versus one.
Distributing a task where most of the time is spent shuffling data between nodes rather than computing.
Assuming linear speedup — doubling nodes rarely exactly doubles speed due to coordination overhead.
ds_usage: The conceptual foundation for every big data tool — Hadoop's HDFS and MapReduce, Spark's cluster execution model, and distributed databases all exist because distributed computing lets organizations process data at a scale no single server could handle.
